subject: Career
title: Playing the Long Game
description: A quick, practical guide to Playing the Long Game.

hook.text: He helped a junior colleague in 2015. In 2024, that person became a VP and offered him a director role.

buildup.text: Networking payoffs are unpredictable and often delayed by years. The ROI is invisible until it isn't.

discovery.text: People who network only when they need something are transparent. And transactional networking repels.

twist.text: The best networkers invest consistently regardless of immediate need. They play infinite games.

climax.text: Build relationships when you don't need them. They'll be there when you do.

punchline.text: Plant seeds today. Harvest in seasons you can't predict.

quiz.question: Why should you network even when you don't need anything?
options: Relationships built early are available when needed later

details.summary: Long-game networking invests in relationships with no immediate transactional goal, trusting that genuine goodwill compounds into opportunities over years and decades. It contrasts with short-term transactional networking that burns out quickly.
details.whyItMatters: The most valuable career opportunities often come from relationships built years before the need arose. Playing the long game creates a reservoir of goodwill that pays dividends unexpectedly.
takeaways: Invest in relationships without expecting an immediate return
Maintain periodic low-effort touchpoints with long-term contacts
Long-game networkers build reputations as genuinely generous people

faq.question: How do you maintain long-game networking relationships without being annoying?
faq.answer: Two to four touchpoints per year is sufficient for most long-game contacts. Share relevant articles, congratulate achievements, or send brief updates about your own career. The key is consistency over years rather than intensity in any single interaction.

faq.question: How do you know if a long-game networking investment is worth continuing?
faq.answer: If the relationship is mutually respectful and occasionally enriching, it is worth maintaining. Not every connection needs to produce tangible outcomes. The connections that seem least likely to pay off often produce the most surprising and valuable opportunities.
